storyBody.heading: Elizabethan Laboratory and the Arrival of an Obsidian Mirror
paragraphs: In the late 16th century, John Dee worked at the edge of astronomy, navigation, and court counsel. Royal, commercial, and scholarly circles in London were already moving objects, books, and natural curiosities from the Americas into elite homes.

The moment that matters here is not the whole life of Dee but a documented ritual context: a reflective tool from New World material culture entered an occult setting where it was handled as a communicative object with spirits.

storyBody.heading: The Dee Session that Defined a Haunted Object
paragraphs: The historical chain begins with the 1580s phase in which Dee and Edward Kelley used mirrors and crystals during angelic communication sessions. That sequence has a clear chronology: preparation, invocation, witnessed response, and repeated notation by participants.

What became important later was not that science accepted spirits as proof. The sequence recorded the object as a repeatable ritual focus: a specific ritual procedure and a specific object used for a specific purpose.

storyBody.heading: Labeling, Provenance, and Memory Fracture
paragraphs: After Dee's death, possession narratives moved through legal and collecting circles. A 17th-century deposition connected the stone to angelic work, and later catalog language from the Peterborough and Walpole line described it as the tool through which spirits were called.
The language of provenance changed the object’s role: "where" it came from became less certain, but "what it meant" widened. That is how one item survives with two histories at once.

storyBody.heading: Museum Transfer and Public Labels
paragraphs: By the 18th and 19th centuries the object entered major collections, then arrived in the British Museum ecosystem as a catalogued occult-associated mirror.
The museum label and display language mattered as strongly as the ancient material itself. A single case card can turn a private ritual tool into an object with a public biography.

storyBody.heading: From Spirit Session to Modern Haunted Lore
paragraphs: Modern mirror-omen traditions reuse this public biography through compression. Instead of preserving every notebook context, the story is now often reduced to a warning pattern: mirror, darkness, and danger.

In oral and digital traditions, the object’s old role becomes generalized: the same mirror logic is detached from a courtroom of documents and relocated into haunted-house storytelling and mirror challenge folklore.
